a: King Zedekiah sent Pashhur son of Malkijah
t: Two envoys, and a siege just begun
p: Zedekiah's messengers are a court official and a priest, sent early in the Babylonian siege.
b: This Pashhur is not the temple officer Pashhur son of Immer who beat Jeremiah (20:1-6). He is an official who appears again when Jeremiah is nearly put to death (38:1). The priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is probably the second priest later executed at Riblah (52:24-27); he also takes a letter from the exiles (29:25-29) and carries a second request to Jeremiah (37:3). The siege began in the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, about January 588 BC (52:4), so this embassy fits the first weeks. Whether chapter 37:3-10 describes the same embassy or a later one, when an Egyptian army briefly drew the Babylonians off, is debated.

a: in line with all his wonders
p: Zedekiah asks for a rescue like the ones in Israel's story, and above all like Jerusalem's escape from Assyria.
b: The Hebrew word for "wonders" (nifla'ot) is the word for the Exodus signs (Exodus 3:20; Exodus 34:10; Joshua 3:5). Zedekiah's request copies Hezekiah's in 701 BC, when Isaiah told the king to ask and an angel struck the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:1-7; 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36). The court believed the city of the LORD's house could not fall (7:4; Micah 3:11). Jeremiah's answer reverses the story: this time the LORD fights on the other side.
r: Exodus 3:20; Exodus 34:10; 2 Kings 19:1-7; 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36; 7:4; Micah 3:11

a: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
p: Jeremiah usually spells the king's name with an r, closer to the Babylonian original.
b: The king's Babylonian name was Nabu-kudurri-usur, "Nabu, guard my heir." Jeremiah and Ezekiel usually write Nebuchadrezzar, which keeps the r; Kings, Chronicles, Daniel and parts of Jeremiah itself write Nebuchadnezzar. The Plain uses the common English form everywhere (see the Nebuchadnezzar topic).

a: turn around the weapons of war
t: Whose weapons, and who is gathered?
p: Two puzzles: how the LORD turns the defenders' weapons, and who "them" is.
b: The first puzzle is the verb. Some read it as the weapons being turned back on the defenders, so that their own arms fail them; others as the defenders' sorties being driven back inside the walls. The second is "I will gather them into the middle of this city." The Hebrew pronoun can mean the weapons, the Chaldeans or the defenders. Readings: the enemy will be brought into the very heart of Jerusalem; or the army will be pulled back into a city that has become a trap. The Plain keeps the pronoun open.

a: with a hand stretched out and a strong arm
p: The phrase that described Israel's rescue from Egypt now describes God's attack on Jerusalem.
b: "A strong hand and an outstretched arm" is the Bible's stock description of the Exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; Deuteronomy 5:15; Deuteronomy 26:8; Exodus 6:6). Here the same power is aimed at Judah, "in anger, in rage and in great wrath," with the pieces of the formula in a different order. Prophets sometimes say the LORD fights as a warrior against his own people, as when Isaiah says his hand is stretched out in anger (Isaiah 5:25).

a: He will not spare them. He will have no pity and no compassion.
p: Spare, pity, have compassion: the LORD's own mercy words, denied.
b: The three verbs are chus (spare), chamal (pity) and racham (have compassion). The last is the root of rachum, "compassionate," the first word of the LORD's self-description at Sinai (Exodus 34:6). The king of Babylon is the one who will show none, and in the same verse the LORD is the one handing them over. Compare Ezekiel 5:11, where the LORD himself says "I will not spare and I will have no pity."

a: the way of life and the way of death
p: Jeremiah's choice echoes Moses' and became a teaching form in Israel and the early church.
b: Moses set "life and death, blessing and curse" before the people (Deuteronomy 30:15, 19); Psalm 1 contrasts two ways, and Proverbs speaks of a path of life (Proverbs 12:28). The early Christian teaching manual called the Didache opens with the same pair, "a way of life and a way of death" (Didache 1:1), and Jesus speaks of two gates (Matthew 7:13-14). In Jeremiah's mouth the choice is concrete and political: stay and die, or go out and live. That is why officials later asked the king to put him to death (38:2-4).
r: Deuteronomy 30:15; Deuteronomy 30:19; Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 12:28; Matthew 7:13-14; Didache 1:1; 38:2-4

a: deserts to the Chaldeans
p: Jeremiah told the besieged to give up, and his enemies called it treason.
b: The Hebrew says someone "falls" to the Chaldeans (naphal 'al), the same verb used of those who defected in 2 Kings 25:11. Jeremiah gives the same advice at 38:2 and 38:17-18, and the officials answer that he is weakening the soldiers' hands (38:4). A Judean military letter from Lachish, written in the same war, says that the words of "the officials" "weaken the hands" of the people; it does not name Jeremiah and does not say where the officials are (Lachish Letter 6, in Torczyner's edition). Jeremiah's advice is not a general rule about governments. It is a word about one siege, and the LORD's own decision (21:10).

a: I have fixed my face on this city
p: God's face fixed on the city is a hostile stare; compare the eyes of 24:6.
b: "To set the face" toward someone is to turn on them (Leviticus 17:10; Leviticus 20:3; Ezekiel 6:2). In 24:6 the LORD says of the good figs, "I will set my eyes on them for good." Amos 9:4 has the opposite: "I will fix my eyes on them for harm and not for good." The fixed look decides whether the people are watched over or watched for judgment.

a: Each morning, give a true verdict.
p: Kings of David's line were expected to hear cases early in the day.
b: Courts sat in the morning, and a king who judged well was a king who kept the covenant with David (2 Samuel 15:2-4; Psalm 101:8; Psalm 72:1-4). The command is addressed to the "house of David" as a whole, the royal family and the officials who ran the courts, not to one king. Jeremiah 22:2-3 partly repeats it (both say "pull the robbed man out of the oppressor's hand"), which is why the two passages are often studied together as the start of his collection of sayings on the kings.

a: you rock on the plain
p: The address is hard: Jerusalem seems meant, and the Greek takes "rock" as a name.
b: Most commentators take the address as Jerusalem, a city set on a rock among valleys, whose people felt untouchable ("Who can come down on us?"). The Greek, as printed in Swete's edition, keeps the Hebrew tsur as a place name ("Sor"), as if "rock" were a title. The boast is the one Zion theology invited: God lives in the city, so no enemy can enter (Psalm 46:5; Psalm 48:3-8), and Micah 3:11 and Jeremiah 7:4 show prophets mocking it.

a: I will set a fire in her forest
p: The "forest" is Jerusalem's cedar-built palaces; 22:6-7 explains.
b: Solomon's palace was called the House of the Forest of Lebanon because of its cedar pillars (1 Kings 7:2-5). Jeremiah calls Jerusalem a forest and sets it on fire; the next chapter makes the picture explicit (22:6-7, 23). The same "fire in the forest" is used of the city's burning at 2 Kings 25:9, when Nebuzaradan set fire to every great house.

a: Go down to the house of the king of Judah
p: Chapters 21:11-23:8 gather sayings about Judah's last rulers, arranged by theme more than by date.
b: The palace stood south of the temple and lower on the ridge, hence "go down." Commentators such as Lundbom and Holladay treat 21:11-23:8 as a booklet on the royal house: first the dynasty as a whole (21:11-22:9), then the kings by name (Shallum, Jehoiakim, Coniah), then the hope of a better shepherd and Branch (23:1-8). The first oracle names no king, so it may belong to the reign of any of Josiah's sons.

a: the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow
p: Foreigner, orphan and widow are the people with no family to speak for them.
b: The same three appear in the Temple Sermon (7:6), in the law (Exodus 22:21-22; Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 24:17) and in the later prophets (Zechariah 7:10). They are the test of whether the king's justice reaches the bottom of society. The Plain matches 7:6 here: "the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow."

a: I have sworn by myself
p: God swears by himself to promise (Genesis 22:16); here he swears to destroy.
b: When God swears by himself, no one is greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The oath usually seals a promise to Abraham or David (Genesis 22:16; Psalm 89:35). Amos (Amos 6:8) and Jeremiah (49:13; 51:14) use it for judgment. The royal house had been given an oath of permanence; Jeremiah answers with an oath on the condition they ignored.

a: You are Gilead to me
t: Gilead and Lebanon: a compliment turned
p: The royal house is praised as the richest, greenest land in the north, then threatened with wilderness.
b: Gilead east of the Jordan and the Lebanon range were known for balm and cedar. The palace complex used Lebanon's cedar lavishly, and 22:23 calls its occupant someone "nested among the cedars." The sentence is an oath form ("if I do not make you a wilderness..."), which the Plain renders as "Surely I will." The beauty of the building is the sign of what will be destroyed.

a: set destroyers apart
p: The Hebrew says the LORD "sanctifies" the attackers: war as holy work.
b: The verb is qiddash, "make holy, set apart." Armies were consecrated before a campaign (6:4; Joel 3:9; Isaiah 13:3), and Jeremiah uses it for the Babylonians against Jerusalem and later for the Medes against Babylon (51:27-28). In his view the invaders are the LORD's tools.

a: Because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD their God
p: Passing nations will ask why the city fell, and the answer is the one Deuteronomy gave.
b: Deuteronomy 29:24-26 pictures the nations asking, "Why has the LORD done this to this land?" and the answer being that the people abandoned the covenant of the LORD. Solomon's temple prayer hears the same question (1 Kings 9:8-9). Jeremiah quotes the script before the disaster happens, so that when it comes the people will understand it as covenant judgment rather than as proof that their God was weak.

a: Weep, weep for the one who is leaving
p: The one to weep for is not the dead king but the one carried off.
b: "The dead man" is most likely Josiah, killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo in 609 BC and mourned by the whole nation (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:24-25). The one who "is leaving" is his son Shallum (verse 11), taken to Egypt. Others read "the dead" as anyone dead and "the one leaving" as exiles in general. The point is that Josiah's death is a closed grief, while the exile of his son opens a longer one.

a: Shallum son of Josiah
p: Shallum was the personal name of the king Kings calls Jehoahaz, who ruled three months in 609 BC.
b: The people of the land made Josiah's younger son king in place of the elder Eliakim, but Pharaoh Neco deposed him after three months, took him to Egypt in chains and made Eliakim king under the new name Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:30-34). First Chronicles 3:15 lists "Shallum" among Josiah's sons. "Jehoahaz" is probably the throne name. Jeremiah's oracle says he will never come back, and Kings agrees that he died in Egypt.

a: Woe to the man
p: Hoy is the funeral cry; here it opens an accusation, and in verse 18 it is the mourning denied.
b: Hoy began as the shout of mourners ("Alas, my brother!" 1 Kings 13:30) and became the prophets' opening for a charge: the dead man walking. Verse 18 uses the same word for the mourning Jehoiakim will be denied. The prophet says "Woe!" over him now so that nobody will say "Alas!" for him later.

a: builds his house
p: Jehoiakim built a grand house with forced labor while Judah paid tribute to Egypt.
b: Jehoiakim had to find a hundred talents of silver for Pharaoh Neco by taxing the people (2 Kings 23:33-35), yet he put up a showy palace with cedar paneling and painted rooms. Forced labor without pay was the abuse Israel had complained of under Solomon and Rehoboam (1 Kings 5:13-18; 1 Kings 12:4). Excavations at Ramat Rahel, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, found a fortified late-monarchy palace with fine stone work; the excavator, Yohanan Aharoni, dated the palace to about 600 BC and linked it with Jehoiakim and with Jeremiah 22:14 (his reports, 1962 and 1964). Later excavations are summarized by Lipschits, Gadot, Arubas and Oeming (2011), and the date and the link with Jehoiakim are still debated.

a: competing in cedar
p: The verb is rare and means "rival" or "burn with rivalry"; the Greek read a different word here.
b: The Hebrew verb (mithareh) comes from charah, "to burn" (as in anger). It is used of rivalry in Jeremiah 12:5 ("how can you compete with horses?"). The sense is: Is it building more cedar halls than your neighbors that makes a king? Swete's Greek reads "Ahaz" where the Hebrew reads "cedar" (see the variant), which would turn the line into a comparison with a bad king.

a: Is this not knowing me?
t: To know God is to do justice
p: In Jeremiah, knowing the LORD is not an inner feeling or a fact learned. It is how the poor are treated.
b: Josiah "knew" the LORD by defending the poor. The idea runs through the prophets: no knowledge of God in the land means no loyalty and no justice (Hosea 4:1-2), and the LORD desires knowledge of him more than burnt offerings (Hosea 6:6). It returns in 9:24 ("let the one who boasts boast in understanding and knowing me") and in the new covenant (31:34), where everyone knows him.

a: Alas, my brother!
t: The mourning he will not get
p: Mourners would cry "Alas" for a king; for Jehoiakim no one will.
b: In a royal funeral the people cried for the dead king as "lord" and called his "majesty" (hod) lost, and relatives said "my brother, my sister" (compare 34:5, where Zedekiah is promised the mourning Jehoiakim is denied). Swete's Greek lacks "my sister" and "his majesty" (see the variants). 4QJer-c supports the longer Hebrew at both places.

a: the way a donkey is buried
p: Sources disagree about the end of Jehoiakim: a quiet death, capture, or an unburied body.
b: Kings says only that Jehoiakim "lay down with his ancestors" (2 Kings 24:6). Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6). Jeremiah 36:30 says his body will be thrown out to the heat by day and the frost by night. Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar killed him and ordered his body thrown outside the wall (Antiquities 10.6.3). The Babylonian Chronicle records only the capture of Jerusalem in March 597 and the king set in place (Grayson). Some read Kings' formula as meaning an ordinary death and burial, so that Jeremiah's threat was not fulfilled as spoken; others think the formula says only that he died.

a: Abarim
p: North, northeast and east: the places from which the city's allies once seemed to come.
b: Lebanon, Bashan and the mountains of Abarim in Moab name the ranges around Judah's borders on three sides. "Your lovers" are allies, Egypt, Assyria and Judah's neighbors, whom Judah chased as the faithless wife chases lovers (2:25; 4:30; Hosea 2:5-13; Ezekiel 16:33-37). Swete's Greek translates "Abarim" as "the far side of the sea."

a: Wind will graze all your shepherds
p: The Hebrew plays on the word for a shepherd and the word for a friend.
b: Tir'eh ruach kol-ro'ayikh uses the verb "shepherd" (ra'ah) for the wind, and "your shepherds" can also be vocalized "your companions" (re'ayikh). The "shepherds" are Judah's rulers and, by extension, her allies. The wind is the sign of nothing: Ephraim "feeds on wind" in Hosea 12:1.

a: Coniah son of Jehoiakim
p: One king, three spellings: Jehoiachin reigned three months and spent his life in Babylon.
b: He is Jehoiachin in Kings and Chronicles, Jeconiah in 24:1, 27:20, 28:4, 29:2 and Matthew 1:11-12, and Coniah here and in verse 28. He became king in December 598 BC as Nebuchadnezzar approached, and surrendered Jerusalem on 2 Adar (16 March 597 BC), according to the Babylonian Chronicle. He was taken to Babylon with his mother, wives and court (2 Kings 24:8-17). Cuneiform ration tablets from Babylon list oil rations for "Ya'ukin, king of Judah" and five of his sons (Weidner). Evil-Merodach released him from prison in 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27-30; 52:31-34).

a: the seal ring on my right hand
t: A signet ring, taken off and later restored
p: A signet ring stands for royal authority; Haggai later makes Jeconiah's grandson the LORD's signet.
b: A signet ring sealed documents and so stood for the owner's authority (Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:10; Song of Songs 8:6). God is saying that even if the king were his own authority, he would pull him off. In Haggai 2:23 the LORD takes Zerubbabel, grandson of Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19), and makes him "like a signet ring," which most commentators read as a reversal of this verse. Sirach 49:11 (a deuterocanonical book) repeats the image of Zerubbabel as the signet on the right hand.

a: the mother who gave birth to you
p: The queen mother shared the throne's fate and was deported with her son.
b: The king's mother held a title (gevirah, "great lady") and a place at court (1 Kings 15:13; Jeremiah 13:18). Nehushta daughter of Elnathan, Jehoiachin's mother (2 Kings 24:8), was taken to Babylon with him (2 Kings 24:12, 15; Jeremiah 29:2). The oracle says both will die there.

a: a despised, shattered jar
t: A vessel no one delights in
p: The same "vessel no one delights in" is used of Israel in Hosea and of Moab later in this book.
b: The Hebrew phrase keli ein hefets bo is the one used of Israel in Hosea 8:8 and of Moab in Jeremiah 48:38. The first word of the verse, nivzeh, adds "despised." The jar image anticipates the potter and broken jar chapters (18-19), and the smashed pot becomes the book's sign for Judah's end (19:10-11). A pot can be discarded; the question raised by Matthew 1:11-12 is whether the line can be.

a: none of his offspring will prosper
t: Jeconiah's curse, Jewish and Christian readings
p: No descendant of Jehoiachin will rule in Judah. How that fits Zerubbabel and Jesus is answered differently.
b: As written, the verse says no son of Jehoiachin will sit on the throne "and rule again in Judah." It was true to the letter: Zedekiah, the next king, was his uncle (2 Kings 24:17), and no later descendant ruled as king. Radak argues that Jeconiah's sons were "childless" because they died in his lifetime and that, because he repented in prison, the decree was lifted, so Zerubbabel could lead Judah. The New Testament lists Jeconiah in Jesus' line (Matthew 1:11-12). Christian answers: the curse affects only a throne ruled by his bloodline and Jesus' kingship comes from God, not from succession; Joseph was only the legal father; Luke's genealogy gives Mary's line through David's son Nathan (Luke 3:31); or the curse was reversed in Haggai 2:23. The Jewish objection is that a Davidic claim passes through the father, so that a messiah cannot descend from Jeconiah. See the chapter page.

a: as one who sits on David's throne
p: The Hebrew joins "prosper" to a participle, "sitting," and the debate over Jeconiah turns on it.
b: The Hebrew says that none of his offspring will "prosper" as one who is sitting (yoshev, a participle) on David's throne and ruling again in Judah. The Plain keeps the participle and the link with "prosper" (yitslach), because the debate turns on it: a flat ban on any descendant ever sitting there, or a statement that none will succeed as a reigning king (which a governor like Zerubbabel would not break). A different oracle, 36:30, bars Jehoiakim's line from David's throne in its own words ("No one belonging to him will sit on David's throne").
orig: יֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא דָוִד (yoshev al kisse David)

a: Woe to the shepherds
p: In the ancient Near East a king was a shepherd; Jeremiah accuses the last kings of losing the flock.
b: The title "shepherd" was used of kings from Mesopotamia and Egypt through Israel (2 Samuel 5:2; Isaiah 44:28). Here it describes the Davidic kings and officials who had failed to guard the people. Ezekiel 34 expands the charge and promises the LORD himself as shepherd, with David as his servant-prince; Zechariah 10-11 develops it, and John 10 has Jesus call himself the good shepherd.

a: You have not paid attention to them. Now I am about to pay attention to you
p: One verb, "attend to," means care in one place and punishment in another; Jeremiah plays on it.
b: Paqad means "visit, give attention to": it can mean taking care of someone (Exodus 3:16, where God visits Israel in Egypt) or calling them to account (as here). The shepherds did not attend to the sheep, so God will attend to the shepherds. The same verb returns in "missing" (23:4), "punished" (23:12) and "I will punish" (23:34).

a: what is left of my flock
p: The remnant is to be gathered from every land where they were driven, not only from Babylon.
b: The promise speaks of "all the lands," which reaches beyond the Babylonian exile to the scattered Judeans in Egypt and elsewhere (24:8-10; 44:1). Christians and Jews have read it differently: as the return under Cyrus (539-538 BC), as a continuing gathering of Israel (Jewish tradition and many Christian readers), or as the gathering of the church. Compare Isaiah 11:11-12 and Ezekiel 34:11-16.

a: a righteous Branch
p: A shoot from David's stump: a righteous king, read as the Messiah or as an ideal ruler.
b: The Hebrew tsemach means a shoot or sprout; the picture is of new growth from a cut-down family tree (Isaiah 11:1 uses a different word). Jeremiah repeats it at 33:15; Zechariah uses it as a name (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12). The Greek translates it anatole, "rising, sunrise," which lies behind Zechariah's song in Luke 1:78. Jewish tradition reads a messiah: the Targum has "a Messiah of the righteous," and Radak says the Branch is the Messiah. Christians read Jesus, son of David. Many critics see a hope for a restored Davidic king at the time of Zedekiah, or for Zerubbabel (Zechariah 6:12).

a: show good sense
p: The Hebrew verb can mean "be wise" or "succeed"; Radak glosses it as "succeed."
b: Hiskil is used of insight and of the success insight brings (Deuteronomy 29:9; Joshua 1:7; Isaiah 52:13). The Plain keeps the wisdom sense and puts "succeed" in the note. The wise, successful king does "justice and righteousness," the two things Jehoiakim lacked (22:13-17).

a: This is the name by which he will be called
t: "The LORD is our righteousness" and the name Zedekiah
p: The name sounds like King Zedekiah's name reversed; readers differ on who bears it and what it claims.
b: The Hebrew YHWH tsidqenu is the name "Zedekiah" (tsidqiyyahu, "my righteousness is the LORD") turned around. Nebuchadnezzar gave Mattaniah that throne name (2 Kings 24:17), and the last king failed it. The coming king will truly be what the name says. Rashi explains: "The LORD will vindicate us in this one's days." Many Christians hear a claim that the Messiah is the LORD himself; Jewish readers hear a name that describes what the LORD will do for the people in his days. At 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem, not the king. See the "Where Christians differ" card on how the LORD becomes our righteousness. The two oracles also differ in the Hebrew in ways the Plain shows: 23:5 "raise up ... a righteous Branch" (tsemach tsaddiq) against 33:15 "make ... sprout" and "a Branch of righteousness" (tsemach tsedaqah); 23:6 "Judah ... and Israel" and "he" against 33:16 "Judah ... and Jerusalem" and "she"; and 23:6 "which anyone will call him" against 33:16 "which anyone will call her." Where the Hebrew is the same (mishpat utsdaqah baarets; yishkon / tishkon lavetach), 33:15-16 should read as 23:5-6 does.

a: As the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up from the land of Egypt
p: The Exodus oath will be eclipsed by a greater homecoming; the same oracle appears at 16:14-15.
b: "As the LORD lives" was the form of a serious oath, and the Exodus was its commonest content. The prophet says that people will stop swearing by the Exodus and start swearing by the return from the north. Most readers take this as comparative: the second event will so surpass the first that the first will seem small, not that Israel will forget Egypt (compare Isaiah 43:16-19). The same two verses stand at 16:14-15, which is the model for the wording. The differences in the Hebrew: 16:15 says "the Israelites" (bene Yisrael), 23:8 "the offspring of the house of Israel" (zera' bet Yisrael); 16:15 speaks of the LORD in the third person ("where he had driven them") and 23:8 in the first ("where I drove them"); 23:8 adds "and brought back" and ends "they will live on their own soil" where 16:15 has "I will return them to the soil I gave to their ancestors."

a: all my bones tremble
p: The Hebrew verb for "tremble" also describes the Spirit's hovering at creation.
b: Rachaph is used only three times in the Bible: here, of Jeremiah's bones; of the Spirit hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2); and of an eagle hovering over its young (Deuteronomy 32:11). Jeremiah is shaken physically by God's holy words, like a man wine has swamped. Compare the fire he cannot hold in (20:9).

a: Under the curse
p: The Hebrew alah means both "curse" and "oath"; the land dries up under the covenant curse.
b: The word can mean the sworn curse of the covenant (Deuteronomy 29:19-21) or a plain oath. Jeremiah's drought language (12:4; 14:2-6) fits the covenant curse. Swete's Greek lacks the clause about adulterers and the curse (see the variant).

a: they prophesied by Baal
p: Samaria's prophets spoke in Baal's name; the Jerusalem prophets, who spoke in the LORD's name, are called worse.
b: Ahab and Jezebel brought hundreds of Baal's prophets to Samaria (1 Kings 18:19-22; 2 Kings 10:18-28), and Hosea condemns Israel for chasing the Baals (Hosea 2:13). Jeremiah compares: the northern prophets were simply apostate, but the Jerusalem prophets use the LORD's name to bless sin (23:14).

a: All of them are like Sodom to me
p: Sodom is the Bible's standard comparison for a city beyond repair; here the charge falls on the prophets.
b: The Hebrew has a simile (kisdom, ka'amorah): "like Sodom," "like Gomorrah." Prophets compare Jerusalem to Sodom (Isaiah 1:9-10; Ezekiel 16:46-56). Jeremiah's reason is different: the prophets "put strength into the hands of evildoers," so that not one gives up his evil. The sin is not only what the prophets do but what they permit by saying all is well. Compare Genesis 18, where Abraham bargains for the city if even ten righteous people are found.

a: wormwood
p: Wormwood is a bitter plant; with poisoned water it stands for the prophets' lies turned back on them.
b: La'anah (wormwood) and rosh (a bitter, poisonous plant) appear together in Deuteronomy 29:18 as the fruit of a heart turned from God. Jeremiah promises the same food and drink to the people in 9:15, and Lamentations 3:15, 19 uses it for the writer's suffering. In Revelation a star called Wormwood poisons a third of the waters (Revelation 8:11).

a: They are leading you into emptiness.
p: The verb comes from hevel, "vapor"; the prophets fill the people with nothing.
b: Mahbilim is related to hevel, the word Ecclesiastes makes famous as "vapor." Jeremiah uses the noun for idols as "vapor" (2:5; 10:3, 15). Those who follow nothing become nothing (2:5). The people are turned into the empty thing they follow.

a: not from the mouth of the LORD
p: A true prophet speaks what the LORD said; a false one speaks from his own heart.
b: Deuteronomy gives tests: a prophet who tempts the people to other gods is false (Deuteronomy 13:1-5), and one whose word does not come true is false (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). Jeremiah adds the source test. Compare Ezekiel 13:2-3, 17, "prophets who prophesy out of their own hearts," and Numbers 16:28, where Moses says he acted "not of my own heart."

a: You will have peace
p: The prophets' message was "shalom," peace; Jeremiah says it was a lie the people liked.
b: "Peace, peace, when there is no peace" (6:14; 8:11) names the same message. Ezekiel too says the prophets whitewash the wall and say "Peace" (Ezekiel 13:10, 16). Chapter 28 shows it in a person, the prophet Hananiah. The Greek of this verse has "those who reject the word of the LORD," where the Hebrew has "those who despise me" (Swete's text): the Greek may have read the Hebrew word for "despise" with the next word as a single phrase.

a: the council of the LORD
p: A true prophet has stood in God's council, the heavenly court, and heard its decision.
b: Sod is the circle of those who deliberate with God: the assembly of the holy ones (Psalm 89:7), the heavenly court in which a spirit volunteers to deceive Ahab (1 Kings 22:19-23), Isaiah's vision of the throne room (Isaiah 6). Amos says God does nothing without telling his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). In Jeremiah's view, a prophet who has not stood there has no message. In 23:22 the true prophet's task, after hearing, is to bring the people back.

a: In the last days you will understand it fully
t: The last days, and the same oracle twice
p: "The last days" can mean the end of history or just a later time; the oracle repeats at 30:23-24.
b: Acharit hayamim, "the end of the days," can mean simply "in time to come" (Genesis 49:1; Deuteronomy 31:29) or the final age (Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14). Here the thought is that the plan of the LORD will be clear in hindsight. Verses 19-20 are repeated at 30:23-24, and 23:19-20 is the model for the wording. In verse 19 the Hebrew differs only in "and a storm, whirling" (vesa'ar mitcholel) here against "a storm, whirling" (sa'ar mitgorer) at 30:23; Swete's Greek has an "earthquake" (seismos) for the storm. In verse 20 there is "burning anger" at 30:24 where 23:20 has only "anger," and 23:20 ends "you will understand it fully" (binah) where 30:24 stops at "understand it."

a: Am I a God at close range
p: God is both close and far, and cannot be hidden from.
b: The question asserts that God is not a local god (compare 1 Kings 20:23-28, where Aram thinks Israel's God is a god of hills). Verse 24 adds that he fills heaven and earth (compare 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 139:7-12; Isaiah 66:1). Paul quotes the nearness in Acts 17:27-28. The Greek says "a God who draws near."

a: I had a dream! I had a dream!
p: Dreams were an accepted way for God to speak, which is why claiming one was so useful.
b: Numbers 12:6 says the LORD speaks to prophets in visions and dreams, and Joel 2:28 promises dreams for all. Jeremiah's complaint is not about dreams as such. He warns against dreamers who put their own wishes in God's mouth (27:9; 29:8; Zechariah 10:2). Verse 28 allows the dream-prophet to tell the dream: the fault is calling it the word of the LORD.

a: Is there anything in the heart
p: The Hebrew question is difficult; the Plain keeps its shape and notes the other readings.
b: The words ha-yesh be-lev are "Is there in the heart...?" The sentence has no clear continuation, so translators supply different things: "Is there any truth in the heart of the lying prophets?" or "How long will lies be in their heart?" The Greek has "How long will it be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies..." The Plain follows the Hebrew and leaves the question open.

a: forgot my name for Baal
p: To forget the LORD's name for Baal's is the oldest charge in Israel's history, and it is about names.
b: Judges describes the generation that forgot the LORD and served the Baals (Judges 2:11-13; Judges 8:33-34). Hosea promises a day when Israel will call the LORD "my husband" and no more "my Baal," since the Baals' names will be removed (Hosea 2:16-17). "Baal" also means "lord" or "husband," which made it easy to give the LORD a Baal's attributes.

a: Is my word not like fire
p: God's word burns and breaks; the rabbis took the hammer as a picture of many meanings.
b: The picture returns to Jeremiah's own experience of the word as a fire in his bones (20:9; 5:14). Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is sharper than a two-edged sword. The Talmud takes the "hammer that breaks the rock" to teach that, as a hammer strikes many sparks from one stone, one verse yields many meanings (Bavli Sanhedrin 34a).

a: announce, "He declares."
p: The Hebrew says they "take their tongues and declare a declaration," using the LORD's own formula.
b: The phrase ne'um YHWH, "the LORD declares," is the prophets' signature. Here the prophets use it as a verb (vayyin'amu ne'um) with no LORD behind it. Verses 30-31 are missing in the Greek (see the variants).

a: What is the oracle of the LORD?
t: Oracle or burden? The word massa'
p: The Hebrew massa' means both "oracle" and "load," and the passage plays on both until the people are the load.
b: Massa' comes from nasa', "lift." It names a "lifting" of the voice, an oracle (Isaiah 13:1; Proverbs 30:1), and a load that is lifted and carried (Numbers 4:15; 2 Kings 5:17). The KJV chose "burden" here. People asked Jeremiah, "What is the massa' of the LORD?" in a mocking tone, as if his prophecies were heavy talk. The MT answers "What massa'?" and promises to throw them off. The Greek and Rashi hear "You are the burden": the people are the load the LORD will set down. The Plain says "oracle" everywhere and notes the other sense here. Verse 39 plays on nasa' a third time.

a: each man's own word will become his oracle
t: A man's word as his load
p: When people use God's name for their own words, the words become their own burden.
b: The ban on saying "the oracle of the LORD" is not a ban on prophecy. People may say, "What has the LORD answered?" (verse 35) but must not label their own opinions with the formula. The punishment fits the offence: whoever sticks "oracle of the LORD" onto his own word must carry that word as a load.

a: utterly forget you
p: The Hebrew has the verbs "forget" (nashah) and "lift" (nasa') in play, completing the pun on the burden.
b: The text as pointed reads venashiti with an infinitive nasho, "I will surely forget you." The Greek has "I will take you up and throw you down," reading the verb as nasa' ("lift"). The pointed text and the Greek may both be understood as the same pun: God "lifts" the load and drops it. The Plain follows the pointed Hebrew.

a: set in front of the LORD's temple
p: Baskets of fruit set before the temple recall first-fruit offerings.
b: The Law told worshipers to bring a basket of first fruits to the place the LORD chose (Deuteronomy 26:1-4). Jeremiah sees the baskets in a vision beside the temple, perhaps as offerings. The pun in Amos 8:1-2, where a basket of summer fruit (qayits) announces the end (qets), shows prophets reading ordinary fruit as signs, as Jeremiah did with the almond branch (1:11-14). The date is after 597 BC (the deportation of Jeconiah) and before 586, during Zedekiah's reign.

a: the first figs of the season
p: The first figs of the season were prized as the best, a treat people picked and ate at once.
b: Bikkurot are the first ripe figs of the season (Isaiah 28:4; Micah 7:1). Hosea 9:10 says that the LORD found Israel like "the first fruit on the fig tree." Bad figs, by contrast, were ones that rotted or dried up and went unpicked.

a: acknowledge the exiles of Judah
t: Which Judeans are the good figs?
p: The vision says the exiles of 597 BC, not those left in Jerusalem, are the good figs.
b: This reverses what the people in Jerusalem thought. Those left behind took their escape as favor and the exiles as outcasts (Ezekiel 11:15). Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (chapter 29) says the same as this vision. Many critical scholars (Carroll, for example) think the chapter comes from the exiles' own point of view and treats them as the true Israel; traditional readers take it as Jeremiah's own word to Zedekiah's court. The Plain's "acknowledge" renders a verb meaning "recognize" or "treat as one's own." The figs describe groups, not each person: chapter 29 also names exiles who were false prophets (29:21-23).

a: set my eyes on them for good
t: Eyes for good, face for harm
p: The LORD's gaze, set against Jerusalem in 21:10, is set for good on the exiles.
b: In 21:10 the LORD fixed his face on the city for harm. Here his eyes rest on the exiles for good. Amos 9:4 shows the other side: eyes fixed for harm and not for good. Deuteronomy 11:12 says the land is one whose "eyes of the LORD your God are always on it."

a: I will build them up and not demolish them
p: Four of the six verbs of Jeremiah's call (1:10) return here as promises for the exiles.
b: At his call Jeremiah is sent "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (1:10). The exiles are promised building and planting, with no demolishing and no pulling up; the same verbs recur in 31:28, 42:10 and 45:4. The words mean the book's theme (judgment then restoration) is being applied to a particular group.

a: a heart to know me
p: The people are to return with their whole heart, and God must first give the heart.
b: The new heart anticipates the new covenant (31:33) and Ezekiel's heart of flesh (Ezekiel 11:19; Ezekiel 36:26). God gives the heart that can return to him, just as in Lamentations 5:21: "Bring us back to yourself, LORD, and we will come back." Deuteronomy 30:6 has the same idea: God circumcises the heart. Compare the heart that is "deceitful above all things" in 17:9.

a: They will become my people, and I will become their God
p: "My people, your God" is the covenant formula; it returns in the new covenant and in Revelation.
b: The words are the heart of the covenant bond (Leviticus 26:12). Jeremiah uses them at 7:23, 11:4, 30:22, 31:33 and 32:38; Ezekiel at Ezekiel 36:28 and Ezekiel 37:27; Zechariah at Zechariah 8:8. Paul applies them to the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation 21:3 gives them as the last promise.

a: those who live in the land of Egypt
p: Some Judeans had fled or been sent to Egypt before 586; they are named among the bad figs.
b: Zedekiah's policy leaned on Egypt (37:5-7; Ezekiel 17:15), and some Judeans emigrated, such as Uriah the prophet, who fled to Egypt and was brought back and killed (26:20-23). After the fall, a larger group went to Egypt against Jeremiah's advice (chapters 42-44). Exiles in Egypt and Babylon thus stand on opposite sides of this chapter.

a: a byword, a taunt and a curse
p: The list of insults (horror, byword, taunt, curse) comes from the curses of Deuteronomy.
b: Deuteronomy 28:37 warns that Israel would become a horror, a saying and a byword among all the peoples. Solomon's dedication prayer hears the same threat (1 Kings 9:7). Jeremiah repeats the formula at 25:18, 29:18 and 44:8. Zechariah reverses it: those who were a curse among the nations will be a blessing (Zechariah 8:13).

a: the sword, the famine and the disease
t: The three diseases of the book
p: Sword, famine and disease (dever) are Jeremiah's fixed triad, from the covenant curses.
b: The triad appears about a dozen times (14:12; 21:7, 9; 27:8, 13; 29:17-18; 32:24, 36; 38:2; 42:17, 22; 44:13). Leviticus 26:25-26 already lists sword, plague and hunger. Dever is "disease," the kind that spreads and kills in a besieged city. The Greek of this verse reads "famine, death, sword" in a different order and renders dever as "death" (Swete's text). Greek 24:9 differs too: it has "dispersion... reproach, a byword, hatred and a curse" (see the variant).

a: in the fourth year of Jehoiakim
t: 605-604 BC: Carchemish and the new king
p: Jehoiakim's fourth year, Nebuchadnezzar's first, is the year Babylon became master of the region.
b: In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish (46:2) and took the throne at his father's death. According to the Babylonian Chronicle, the next year he marched through the land of Hatti and took Ashkelon (Grayson). Jehoiakim became his vassal for three years (2 Kings 24:1). The synchronism is correct if Judah counted regnal years from autumn and Babylon from spring, and scholars differ on how the systems line up; the usual date is 605-604 BC. Jeremiah 36:1 puts the dictation of the first scroll in the same year. The Greek lacks the clause "That was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar" (see the variant).

a: getting up early to speak
p: "Getting up early" is Jeremiah's phrase for God's persistent sending of prophets.
b: The Hebrew verb (hashkem) pictures someone who gets up at dawn to do something. It occurs in 7:13, 25; 11:7; 25:3-4; 26:5; 29:19; 32:33; 35:14-15; 44:4 and in 2 Chronicles 36:15, always of God's patient sending of messengers and of the people's refusal to listen.

a: his servants the prophets
p: "His servants the prophets" is a repeated phrase in Kings and Jeremiah.
b: The same formula runs through Jeremiah (7:25; 26:5; 29:19; 35:15; 44:4) and through the Deuteronomistic History (2 Kings 17:13, 23; 2 Kings 21:10; 2 Kings 24:2), as well as Amos 3:7 and Zechariah 1:6. Critical scholars see this prose sermon as shaped by the Deuteronomistic school (Thiel, Nicholson) from a core of Jeremiah's words, while others argue it comes from Jeremiah or Baruch (Bright, Holladay).

a: turn back
p: "Turn back" (shuvu) and "live" (veshevu) sound alike; turning back is how they stay.
b: The Hebrew has shuvu na... veshevu 'al ha'adamah, "turn back... and live on the land." The sounds echo each other, and the root shuv is the book's key word for turning back or away (3:12-14; 8:4-5). The promise of the land "from long ago to forever" (le'olam ve-ad olam) is conditioned on turning back.

a: my servant
p: A pagan conqueror is called the LORD's servant; the claim shocked Judah's leaders.
b: Jeremiah repeats the title at 27:6 and 43:10. "Servant" (eved) was a title for a king's vassal or agent. Isaiah called Assyria the rod of the LORD's anger (Isaiah 10:5) and Cyrus his anointed (Isaiah 45:1). Habakkuk asks how God can use a nation worse than Judah (Habakkuk 1:6, 13). Many in Judah called Jeremiah a traitor. The Greek of this verse lacks the whole phrase (see the variant).

a: put them under the ban
p: The ban (cherem) was the destruction of a city given wholly to God; here it falls on Judah and her neighbors.
b: The ban in Israel's war law covered Jericho and the Canaanite cities (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:17-21). To apply it to Judah and the nations is to treat God's people like the Canaanites. The Plain uses "put under the ban" for cherem.

a: the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
p: The loss of wedding songs, grinding and lamplight sums up a land emptied of life.
b: Jeremiah uses the line four times: 7:34, 16:9, 25:10 and, as a promise of its return, 33:10-11. Revelation 18:22-23 applies it to Babylon the Great: no lamp, no millstone, no voice of bridegroom and bride. The hand mill was a woman's morning task (Exodus 11:5), so its silence means no one is left to eat.

a: seventy years
t: The seventy years: how they are counted
p: Four main ways to count seventy years; each has a Bible text behind it.
b: (1) Babylon's domination, about 605 to 539 BC, which is the plain sense of "these nations will serve the king of Babylon." (2) The temple's ruin to its rebuilding, 586 to 516 BC, which suits Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5. (3) Chronicles counts the seventy years as the land's sabbath rest (2 Chronicles 36:21, quoting Leviticus 26:34-35). (4) A round number: seventy is a lifetime (Psalm 90:10), Isaiah 23:15 speaks of seventy years for Tyre, and an inscription of Esarhaddon says Marduk planned seventy years of desolation for Babylon and then shortened them to eleven (Borger). Daniel 9:2, 24 reads the seventy years again as seventy weeks of years. Jeremiah 29:10 repeats the number in his letter to the exiles.

a: When the seventy years are over
p: Babylon, the LORD's tool, is itself brought to account; the fall comes in chapters 50-51.
b: "I will punish the king of Babylon" uses the same verb, paqad, as 23:2. Babylon fell to Cyrus in October 539 BC, and 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 and Ezra 1:1 present Cyrus's decree as the fulfilment of Jeremiah's word. The fuller oracle is in chapters 50-51. Whether "a wasteland forever" was fulfilled in stages, as poetry, or is still to come is discussed there.

a: all that is written in this book
p: "This book" may be the first scroll, or the book as a whole; the Greek changes what follows.
b: Some commentators take "this book" as the scroll Jeremiah dictated in the same year (36:1-4, 32); others as the finished book, with this verse as the end of an early edition. Hebrew goes on to say the book is "what Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations," which leads into the oracles against the nations (46-51). In the Greek the oracles against the nations follow right here (Greek 25:14-31:44 in Swete's numbering), and the clause "what Jeremiah prophesied against the nations" serves there as the heading of that block, without "all" (see the variant). This is part of the case for two editions; see the chapter page.

a: worked as slaves by many nations and great kings
p: Babylon, which made others serve, will be made to serve in its turn; 27:7 says the same in other words.
b: The Hebrew verb is the same as in 27:7 ('avdu / we'avdu b-). The Plain here reads "worked as slaves by"; 27:7 reads "make him their slave," and should match this earlier text. The "they" of this verse is most likely Babylon and the nations it ruled. Some scholars see verse 14 as a later addition drawing on 27:7 and 50:29 and 51:24.

a: Take this cup, the wine of rage
p: A cup of wine that makes the nations drunk and sick: a picture of judgment found across the Bible.
b: The cup of the LORD's rage appears in Isaiah 51:17-22, Psalm 75:8, Habakkuk 2:15-16, Ezekiel 23:31-34 and Obadiah 16; Jeremiah repeats it at 49:12 and 51:7. In the New Testament, Revelation 14:10 and 16:19 take it up. Christian readers also hear it in Jesus' Gethsemane prayer, "if it can be done, let this cup go past me" (Matthew 26:39), where Jesus takes the cup meant for others. Jewish readers take the cup as the judgment on the nations that Jeremiah announces.
r: Isaiah 51:17-22; Psalm 75:8; Habakkuk 2:15-16; Ezekiel 23:31-34; 49:12; 51:7; Revelation 14:10; Matthew 26:39

a: made all the nations drink it
t: A vision, an act, or a message?
p: Jeremiah cannot literally visit every nation; commentators read the cup as a vision, an acted sign or a spoken oracle.
b: Jeremiah says he took the cup and made the nations drink it, yet his own list reaches from Egypt to Elam. Commentators read it as (1) a vision in which he saw himself serving the cup; (2) a symbolic act, as in chapter 27, when envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon came to Jerusalem and he gave them yokes; or (3) a way of saying that his oracles to the nations (verses 27-38) carried the cup. The Plain keeps Jeremiah's words.

a: as they are today
p: The phrase looks back from after 586 BC and hints that this passage was shaped later.
b: In 605-604 BC Jerusalem and Judah's towns were not yet ruins. "As they are today" (kayyom hazzeh) is the voice of an editor writing after the fall, as at 44:2, 22. Critical scholars use this clause to show that the chapter was reworked. Traditional readers may take it as the prophet's certainty or as a later note by Baruch.

a: all the mixed peoples
p: 'Erev means a mixed company: foreign soldiers, traders or tribes living in a land that is not their own.
b: The word describes the mixed crowd that left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38), the foreign troops in Egypt's army (Jeremiah 50:37; Ezekiel 30:5) and desert tribes. The Greek has symmiktoi, "mixed." Some read it as "Arabs" (the consonants are the same as 'Arab' in verse 24).

a: all who have their hair cut at the corners
t: The peoples with hair cut at the corners
p: A custom of trimming hair at the temples marks certain desert and Arabian peoples.
b: Jeremiah mentions these peoples again at 9:26 and 49:32 (qetsutse pe'ah, "cut at the edge"). The Plain here matches 9:26, the earlier text; 49:32 should read the same. Leviticus 19:27 forbids Israelites to cut the hair at the edge of the head. The Greek historian Herodotus reports that the Arabs shave their hair in a round fashion around the temples (Histories 3.8).

a: Zimri
p: Zimri is an unknown people; Elam and Media lie east, in what is now Iran.
b: Zimri does not appear as a nation elsewhere. A few suggest Zimran (Genesis 25:2), a son of Keturah, but there is no agreement. Elam was the old kingdom east of Babylon (oracle in 49:34-39). Media lay northeast; the Medes joined Babylon against Assyria and later helped Cyrus overthrow Babylon (51:11, 28). Swete's Greek has "Elam and the Persians" here. In 4QJer-c "Zimri" is visible and "Media" is restored.

a: Sheshach
p: "Sheshach" is Babylon (Bavel) written in the letter-swap code called atbash.
b: In atbash the first letter of the alphabet is swapped with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. Babel (B-B-L) becomes Sh-Sh-K. Rashi says "Sheshach is Babylon in atbash." Jeremiah does the same at 51:41, and "Leb-qamai" (51:1) is atbash for "Chaldeans." Reasons suggested: avoiding the name for caution or politeness, a prophet's joke, or a later scribe's addition. The Greek lacks the whole sentence, but 4QJer-c has it. The cipher puts Babylon last in the list of nations that drink. Separately, 51:7 pictures Babylon as a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the whole earth drunk.

a: the city that is called by my name
p: Jerusalem, the city that bears God's name, is the first to be struck.
b: The temple and city are "called by my name" (7:10-14, 30; 14:9; 32:34; Daniel 9:18-19). Ezekiel 9:6 says the destroyers should "begin at my sanctuary," and 1 Peter 4:17 says that judgment starts with God's household. Closeness to God is not a shield but a standard.

a: The LORD will roar from on high
t: The lion's roar and the winepress
p: God roars like a lion from his holy dwelling, and the shout is that of workers treading grapes.
b: Amos 1:2 uses nearly the same words for the LORD roaring from Zion. The shout (hedad) of grape treaders is a harvest song (48:33; Isaiah 16:9-10), here turned into a war cry. Isaiah 63:1-6 and Revelation 14:19-20 and 19:15 treat judgment as treading a winepress.

a: the LORD has a case against the nations
p: Riv is a legal case: the LORD takes the nations to court.
b: Prophets often picture God suing his people (Hosea 4:1; Micah 6:2; Jeremiah 2:9). Here the court is wider, and the defendants are "all flesh." Compare Joel 3:2 and Isaiah 66:16. The verdict is already given: the wicked go to the sword.

a: No one will cry for them, collect them or bury them.
p: Lying unburied is the curse of Deuteronomy and a mark of Jeremiah's judgments.
b: Deuteronomy 28:26 curses Israel with corpses left to birds and beasts. Jeremiah returns to it at 8:2, 9:22 and 16:4-6, and Psalm 79:2-3 laments it. In the ancient world, burial was the last duty of the family and the community; without it the dead were disgraced.

a: Howl, you shepherds, and scream!
p: The "shepherds and lords of the flock" are rulers; they return from 23:1-4 to meet their end.
b: The ruling class of every nation is called "shepherds" and "mighty ones of the flock" (rams), the same figure used in 22:22 and 23:1-4. The final poem has no hope for the shepherds: no escape, no rescue (verse 35), and the pasture itself laid waste (verse 36). Ezekiel 34:2-10 gives the same charge.
